description: Immediate action protocols for acute menopause symptom crises

entries.title: Severe Hot Flash Protocol
entries.description: What to do during an intense hot flash episode
entries.content: Severe hot flashes can feel overwhelming and frightening. Having a protocol helps you regain control and reduce the intensity and duration.
immediate_actions: 1. BREATHE: Start box breathing immediately (Inhale 4, Hold 4, Exhale 4, Hold 4)
2. COOL: Remove layers, use handheld fan, apply cold water to wrists and neck
3. DRINK: Sip cold water or ice water slowly
4. SIT: If possible, sit down and focus on breathing
5. DISTRACT: Count backwards from 100 by 7s to engage your brain
cooling_strategies: Cold water on wrists, neck, face
Handheld battery fan (keep one in purse/desk)
Ice pack or frozen water bottle to hold
what_not_to_do: Don't panic - it will pass (usually 2-5 minutes)
Don't fight it - accept and breathe through it
Don't feel embarrassed - it's a medical symptom
entries.prevention_kit: Keep a 'hot flash kit' ready: handheld fan, cooling towel, water bottle, hair tie (to get hair off neck)
entries.when_to_seek_help: If hot flashes are happening multiple times per hour, preventing sleep, or significantly impacting your life, see your doctor. Effective treatments are available.

entries.title: Panic Attack During Menopause
entries.description: Managing acute anxiety or panic episodes
entries.content: Panic attacks can occur or worsen during menopause due to hormonal effects on stress regulation. They're frightening but not dangerous, and you can manage them.
immediate_actions: 1. RECOGNIZE: Remind yourself 'This is a panic attack, not a heart attack. It will pass.'
2. BREATHE: Box breathing or 4-7-8 breathing (Inhale 4, Hold 7, Exhale 8)
3. GROUND: 5-4-3-2-1 technique (name 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you touch, 2 you smell, 1 you taste)
4. MOVE: If possible, walk slowly or do gentle stretching
5. COLD: Splash cold water on face or hold ice cube (activates dive reflex, calms nervous system)
grounding_techniques: Hold ice cube and focus on sensation
Name objects in the room out loud
Stomp feet to feel connection to ground
breathing_techniques: Belly breathing (hand on stomach, breathe deep)
Counted breathing (count each breath to 10, repeat)
what_to_remember: Panic attacks peak in 10 minutes and pass within 20-30 minutes
You are not dying or going crazy
This is your body's stress response misfiring
Hormonal changes make panic more likely during menopause
Treatment (HRT, therapy, medication) can prevent future attacks
entries.when_to_call_911: If you have chest pain, difficulty breathing that doesn't improve, or are unsure if it's panic or a heart problem, call 911. Better safe than sorry.
entries.follow_up: If panic attacks are recurring, see your doctor. HRT, CBT, and/or anti-anxiety medication can be very effective.

entries.title: Insomnia Crisis (Multiple Sleepless Nights)
entries.description: What to do when you haven't slept in days
entries.content: Multiple nights of severe insomnia can feel desperate. While you need medical help for chronic insomnia, these strategies can help in the short term.
immediate_actions_tonight: 1. ACCEPT: Stop trying to force sleep - it creates more anxiety
2. GET UP: If awake >20 minutes, get up and do something boring (read, listen to calm music)
3. COOL: Keep room very cool (65-68°F) - helps with night sweats and sleep
4. DARK: Ensure complete darkness (blackout curtains, eye mask)
5. QUIET: Use earplugs or white noise if needed
6. NO CLOCK: Turn clock away - watching time increases anxiety
short_term_strategies: Take melatonin 1-2 hours before desired bedtime (1-3mg)
Warm bath or shower 1-2 hours before bed
Guided sleep meditation (apps: Calm, Headspace, Insight Timer)
what_not_to_do: Don't lie in bed awake for hours (creates negative association)
Don't nap during day (makes night sleep worse)
Don't drink alcohol to sleep (causes rebound wakefulness)
Don't catastrophize ('I'll never sleep again') - you will
Don't take Benadryl regularly (tolerance develops, side effects)
entries.crisis_management: If you're on day 3-4 of no sleep, call your doctor. They may prescribe short-term sleep medication while addressing the underlying cause.
underlying_causes: Night sweats (treat with HRT or other medications)
Anxiety (treat with HRT, therapy, or medication)
Poor sleep hygiene (fixable with behavioral changes)
entries.long_term_solution: See doctor for: HRT (if hormonal cause), CBT-I (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia - highly effective), or other treatments. Don't suffer long-term.

entries.title: Severe Mood Episode (Rage or Despair)
entries.content: Intense mood swings, rage, or despair can occur during menopause due to hormonal effects on neurotransmitters. These episodes are real, biological, and manageable.
during_rage_episode: 1. REMOVE: Remove yourself from the situation if possible
2. BREATHE: Deep breathing to activate calm response
3. MOVE: Physical activity helps discharge the energy (walk, run, exercise)
4. COLD: Cold water on face or ice pack can interrupt the rage response
5. WAIT: Don't make decisions or send messages during the episode
6. RELEASE: Scream into pillow, punch pillow, or cry - safe emotional release
during_despair_episode: 1. SAFETY FIRST: If having thoughts of self-harm, call 988 (Suicide Prevention Lifeline) or go to ER
2. REACH OUT: Call trusted friend, family member, or therapist
3. REMIND: 'This is hormones. This feeling will pass. It's not reality.'
4. COMFORT: Wrap in blanket, drink warm tea, gentle self-soothing
5. DISTRACT: Watch comforting show, listen to music, pet an animal
6. WAIT: Don't make major decisions during the episode
grounding_for_intense_emotions: Remind yourself: 'This is a hormonal episode, not reality'
Physical grounding: stomp feet, hold ice, splash cold water
Timed breathing: breathe slowly for 5 minutes
Safe emotional release: cry, scream into pillow, write angry letter (don't send)
crisis_resources: Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741
Emergency room if in immediate danger
entries.important_message: Severe mood episodes during menopause are REAL and BIOLOGICAL. They don't mean you're weak or crazy. They mean you need treatment. Please seek help.

entries.title: Sudden Severe Headache or Migraine
entries.description: When to seek emergency care vs manage at home
entries.content: Headaches and migraines can worsen during menopause due to hormonal fluctuations. Most are manageable at home, but some require emergency care.
red_flags_requiring_er: Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache (worst headache of your life)
Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, or vision changes
Headache with weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking
New severe headache pattern if over 50
migraine_management_at_home: 1. DARK & QUIET: Go to dark, quiet room immediately
2. COLD: Ice pack on forehead or back of neck
3. MEDICATE: Take migraine medication or pain reliever EARLY (waiting makes it worse)
5. CAFFEINE: Small amount of caffeine can help (coffee or tea) if you don't usually consume it
prevention_strategies: Avoid common triggers: alcohol, aged cheese, processed meats, artificial sweeteners
when_to_see_doctor_non_emergency: Headaches occurring more than 2x per week
entries.hormonal_migraine_note: Migraines often worsen during perimenopause due to fluctuating estrogen. HRT (especially transdermal estrogen) can significantly reduce hormonal migraines for many women.

entries.title: Severe Palpitations or Chest Discomfort
entries.description: When to go to ER vs when it's likely hormonal
entries.content: Heart palpitations are common during menopause, but chest pain or severe palpitations require medical evaluation to rule out cardiac issues.
go_to_er_immediately_if: Chest pain or pressure (especially if radiating to arm, jaw, or back)
Palpitations lasting more than a few minutes
Feeling like you might pass out
Chest pain with sweating or nausea
likely_hormonal_palpitations: Brief fluttering sensation (few seconds to 1-2 minutes)
Occurs during hot flash or anxiety
No chest pain or shortness of breath
entries.follow_up_needed: Even if palpitations seem hormonal, see your doctor for ECG to rule out arrhythmias. Better to check and be reassured.
entries.important_distinction: Palpitations = feeling your heartbeat (usually benign). Chest pain = potential emergency. When in doubt, go to ER.

entries.title: Emergency Contacts & Resources
entries.content: Keep these resources readily available for menopause-related emergencies and crises.

crisis_hotlines.use_for: Suicidal thoughts, severe depression, emotional crisis
Any crisis, prefer texting over calling
Medical emergencies, chest pain, severe symptoms
If menopause stress is affecting relationship safety

when_to_use_which: 988/Crisis Line: Suicidal thoughts, severe depression, emotional crisis
911: Chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe headache with neurological symptoms, any life-threatening emergency
ER: Severe symptoms, post-menopausal bleeding, symptoms that might be cardiac
Urgent Care: Severe symptoms during off-hours, need evaluation but not life-threatening
Doctor's Office: Non-emergency symptoms, treatment adjustments, follow-up
Nurse Line: Unsure if symptoms warrant ER, need guidance
